title: Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules

toc.title: 4.1 Electronic theory of valency; ionic, covalent and coordinate bonds; Lewis structures
4.2 VSEPR theory and shapes; valence bond theory, σ and π bonds, hybridisation
4.3 Dipole moment, ionic character of covalent bonds and bond length
4.4 Hydrogen bonding, metallic bonding and van der Waals forces

html:
Chemical bonding carries about two questions in the paper, and its ideas — shape, hybridisation, polarity, hydrogen bonding — reappear in organic, inorganic and states-of-matter questions.

The favourite question types are: the shape or hybridisation of a given molecule or ion, a bond-angle or dipole-moment order, counting σ and π bonds, a Fajans'-rule comparison, and "why does water boil so high?".

One counting formula (the steric number) answers most shape questions in seconds.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Ionic, covalent and coordinate bonds; where coordinate bonds occur (NH₄⁺, H₃O⁺, H₃N→BF₃, O₃, CO, complex ions); exceptions to the octet rule.
  • Steric number = bond pairs + lone pairs on the central atom; fast formula SN = ½(V + M − c + a).
  • Shapes and angles: linear 180°, trigonal planar 120°, tetrahedral 109.5°, NH₃ 107°, H₂O 104.5°, TBP, octahedral, see-saw, T-shape, square planar.
  • Hybridisation sp, sp², sp³, sp³d, sp³d², sp³d³; σ from head-on overlap, π from sideways overlap; single = σ, double = σ + π, triple = σ + 2π.
  • Dipole moment μ = q × d (debye); symmetric molecules have μ = 0; NH₃ > NF₃; % ionic character = μ(observed)/μ(ionic) × 100.
  • Fajans' rules; bond length falls with bond order and with s character.
  • Hydrogen bonding (F, O, N), metallic bonding (electron sea) and van der Waals forces, with their effects on boiling point, solubility and density.

4.1 Electronic theory of valency; ionic, covalent and coordinate bonds; Lewis structures

The electronic theory of valency

Kossel and Lewis (1916) explained bonding by the stability of the noble gases: atoms combine so as to reach a stable noble-gas configuration — eight outer electrons (an octet), or two (a duplet) for H (in H₂), Li⁺ and Be²⁺.

They do this by transferring electrons (ionic bond), by sharing them (covalent bond), or by sharing a pair that one atom supplies (coordinate bond).

Only the valence electrons take part; in a Lewis symbol they are shown as dots round the element symbol.

Ionic, covalent and coordinate bonds

Ionic (electrovalent) Covalent Coordinate (dative)
Formed by complete transfer of electrons mutual sharing of electron pairs sharing of a pair supplied by one atom (donor) to another (acceptor)
Favoured by low IE of the metal, high EA of the non-metal, high lattice energy similar, fairly high electronegativities a lone pair on the donor, a vacant orbital on the acceptor
Example Na⁺Cl⁻, Mg²⁺O²⁻ H₂, Cl₂, CH₄, H₂O NH₄⁺, H₃O⁺, H₃N→BF₃
Directional? no (so no isomerism) yes (so shapes and isomerism) yes
Property Ionic compounds Covalent (molecular) compounds
State and melting point crystalline solids, high mp and bp gases, liquids or soft solids, low mp and bp
Conductivity conduct when molten or in water, not as solids non-conductors (except graphite, and those that ionise in water, like HCl)
Solubility in polar solvents (water) in non-polar solvents (benzene, CCl₄)
Reactions fast (between ions) slow (bonds must break)

Giant covalent solids (diamond, SiO₂) are the exception to "low melting point": every atom is held in a three-dimensional covalent network.

Coordinate bond

A coordinate (dative) bond is a covalent bond in which both shared electrons come from one atom. It is shown by an arrow from the donor to the acceptor, as in H₃N→BF₃. Once formed it is identical to an ordinary covalent bond: all four N–H bonds in NH₄⁺ are the same.

Coordinate bonds occur in NH₄⁺ (H⁺ ← :NH₃), H₃O⁺, H₃N→BF₃, Al₂Cl₆ (two Cl→Al bridges), the complex ions such as [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺, and in the Lewis structures of O₃, CO (C≡O with one dative bond), HNO₃ and N₂O₅.

Lewis structures and formal charge

To draw one: (1) add up the valence electrons (add one for each negative charge, subtract one for each positive charge); (2) put the least electronegative atom (never H) in the centre and join the atoms by single bonds; (3) complete the octets of the outer atoms; (4) put any electrons left on the central atom; (5) if the central atom is still short of an octet, convert lone pairs on neighbours into double or triple bonds.

The best structure has the smallest formal charges:

\text{formal charge} = V - L - \frac{B}{2}

where V = valence electrons of the free atom, L = non-bonding (lone-pair) electrons on it and B = electrons in its bonds.

Formal charges in carbon monoxide

Problem. Find the formal charges in the Lewis structure :C≡O: (one lone pair on each atom, a triple bond).

Solution. C: V = 4, L = 2, B = 6 → 4 − 2 − 3 = −1. O: V = 6, L = 2, B = 6 → 6 − 2 − 3 = +1. The charges oppose the electronegativity difference, which is why CO has a very small dipole moment (about 0.1 D).

Failure of the octet rule Examples
Incomplete octet BeCl₂ (4 electrons round Be), BF₃ and AlCl₃ (6)
Expanded octet (period 3 onwards, using d orbitals) PCl₅ (10), SF₆ (12), IF₇ (14), H₂SO₄ (S has 12)
Odd-electron molecules NO, NO₂, ClO₂
Noble-gas compounds XeF₂, XeF₄, XeF₆, XeO₃

The octet rule also says nothing about the shapes of molecules or the energies of bonds — which is what the next two theories add.

4.2 VSEPR theory and shapes; valence bond theory, σ and π bonds, hybridisation

VSEPR theory

The valence shell electron pair repulsion theory (Sidgwick and Powell; developed by Nyholm and Gillespie) says:

  1. The shape of a molecule depends on the number of electron pairs (bond pairs and lone pairs) round the central atom.
  2. The pairs repel one another and take up positions as far apart as possible.
  3. Repulsion falls in the order lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair, so lone pairs squeeze the bond angles.
  4. A double or triple bond counts as one region (one "pair") for shape.

Steric number (SN) = number of atoms bonded to the central atom + number of lone pairs on it. The fast way to find it:

SN = \frac{1}{2}\left(V + M - c + a\right)

V = valence electrons of the central atom; M = number of monovalent atoms attached (H, F, Cl, Br, I — oxygen and sulphur count as 0); c = charge of a cation; a = charge of an anion. Lone pairs = SN − number of bonded atoms.

The SN also gives the hybridisation: 2 sp, 3 sp², 4 sp³, 5 sp³d, 6 sp³d², 7 sp³d³.

SN Bond pairs Lone pairs Shape Angle Examples
2 2 0 linear 180° BeCl₂, CO₂, HCN, NO₂⁺
3 3 0 trigonal planar 120° BF₃, SO₃, NO₃⁻, CO₃²⁻
3 2 1 bent (V-shaped) < 120° SO₂ (119°), O₃ (117°), NO₂⁻
4 4 0 tetrahedral 109.5° CH₄, CCl₄, NH₄⁺, SO₄²⁻, ClO₄⁻
4 3 1 trigonal pyramidal 107° (NH₃) NH₃, PCl₃, H₃O⁺, XeO₃, ClO₃⁻
4 2 2 bent 104.5° (H₂O) H₂O, H₂S, OF₂, NH₂⁻
5 5 0 trigonal bipyramidal 90°, 120° PCl₅, PF₅
5 4 1 see-saw — SF₄, TeCl₄
5 3 2 T-shaped about 90° ClF₃, BrF₃
5 2 3 linear 180° XeF₂, I₃⁻, ICl₂⁻
6 6 0 octahedral 90° SF₆, PCl₆⁻
6 5 1 square pyramidal — BrF₅, IF₅
6 4 2 square planar 90° XeF₄, ICl₄⁻
7 7 0 pentagonal bipyramidal 72°, 90° IF₇

In a trigonal bipyramid, lone pairs always take the equatorial positions (they have more room there), which is why SF₄ is a see-saw, ClF₃ a T and XeF₂ linear.

Shapes by the counting formula

Problem. Find the hybridisation and shape of SF₄, ClF₃, XeF₄ and NO₃⁻.

Solution. SF₄: ½(6 + 4) = 5 → sp³d; 4 bonded atoms, 1 lone pair → see-saw. ClF₃: ½(7 + 3) = 5 → sp³d; 3 bonded, 2 lone pairs → T-shaped. XeF₄: ½(8 + 4) = 6 → sp³d²; 4 bonded, 2 lone pairs → square planar.

NO₃⁻: ½(5 + 0 + 1) = 3 → sp²; 3 bonded, no lone pair → trigonal planar (O counts 0).

Bond-angle orders worth knowing.

  • Lone pairs squeeze the angle: CH₄ (109.5°) > NH₃ (107°) > H₂O (104.5°).
  • Down a group the central atom becomes less electronegative, the bond pairs sit farther from it and repel less: NH₃ (107°) > PH₃ (93.5°) > AsH₃ (92°); H₂O (104.5°) > H₂S (92°).
  • Electronegative outer atoms pull the bond pairs away from the centre: NF₃ (102°) < NH₃ (107°); OF₂ (103°) < H₂O (104.5°) < Cl₂O (111°, where the large Cl atoms also crowd each other).

Valence bond theory: σ and π bonds

A covalent bond forms when half-filled atomic orbitals of two atoms overlap and the two electrons, of opposite spin, pair up between the nuclei. The greater the overlap, the stronger the bond.

Sigma (σ) bond Pi (π) bond
Overlap head-on, along the internuclear axis (s–s, s–p, p–p, hybrid orbitals) sideways, of parallel p orbitals, above and below the axis
Strength stronger (greater overlap) weaker
Rotation about it free restricted (cis–trans isomerism)
Existence can exist alone forms only after a σ bond
Electron density on the axis above and below the axis (a nodal plane on the axis)

A single bond is one σ; a double bond is σ + π; a triple bond is σ + 2π. Counting examples: C₂H₆ 7σ; C₂H₄ 5σ + 1π; C₂H₂ 3σ + 2π; N₂ 1σ + 2π; CO₂ 2σ + 2π; HCN 2σ + 2π; benzene 12σ + 3π.

Hybridisation

Hybridisation

Hybridisation is the mixing of atomic orbitals of nearly equal energy on the same atom to give the same number of new, equivalent orbitals (hybrid orbitals) with definite directions.

Hybrid orbitals form σ bonds or hold lone pairs; π bonds are formed by the unhybridised p orbitals left over.

Hybridisation Orbitals mixed Geometry Angle s character Examples
sp s + p linear 180° 50 % BeCl₂, C₂H₂, CO₂ (C)
sp² s + 2p trigonal planar 120° 33 % BF₃, C₂H₄, benzene, graphite
sp³ s + 3p tetrahedral 109.5° 25 % CH₄, diamond, NH₃ and H₂O (with lone pairs)
sp³d s + 3p + d trigonal bipyramidal 90°, 120° 20 % PCl₅, SF₄, ClF₃, XeF₂
sp³d² s + 3p + 2d octahedral 90° 17 % SF₆, XeF₄, BrF₅
sp³d³ s + 3p + 3d pentagonal bipyramidal 72°, 90° 14 % IF₇, XeF₆ (distorted)

More s character means a shorter, stronger bond held closer to the nucleus, and a more electronegative atom: sp C > sp² C > sp³ C. That is why ethyne's C–H hydrogen is acidic (Unit 17).

4.3 Dipole moment, ionic character of covalent bonds and bond length

Dipole moment

In a bond between atoms of different electronegativity the shared pair is pulled towards the more electronegative atom, giving partial charges δ+ and δ−. The dipole moment is

\mu = q \times d

(charge × distance). It is a vector; in chemistry its arrow is drawn from the positive towards the negative end. Unit: the debye, 1 D = 3.33 × 10⁻³⁰ C m.

A molecule's dipole moment is the vector sum of its bond moments (and lone-pair moments).

Symmetrical molecules have μ = 0 even with polar bonds: CO₂, BeCl₂, BF₃, CH₄, CCl₄, PCl₅, SF₆, XeF₄, trans-1,2-dichloroethene and p-dichlorobenzene. Bent and pyramidal molecules are polar: H₂O 1.85 D, NH₃ 1.47 D, SO₂, H₂S.

Comparison Order and reason
NH₃ (1.47 D) > NF₃ (0.23 D) in NH₃ the lone-pair moment adds to the N←H bond moments; in NF₃ it opposes the N→F bond moments
HF > HCl > HBr > HI electronegativity difference falls
CH₃Cl > CH₂Cl₂ > CHCl₃ > CCl₄ (= 0) the C–Cl moments cancel more and more as the molecule becomes symmetrical
o- > m- > p-dichlorobenzene (= 0) the angle between the two C–Cl moments widens from 60° to 120° to 180°

Uses: a zero dipole moment proves a symmetrical shape (CO₂ is linear, H₂O is not); the moment measures bond polarity and percentage ionic character:

\%\ \text{ionic character} = \frac{\mu_{\text{observed}}}{\mu_{\text{ionic}}} \times 100, \qquad \mu_{\text{ionic}} = e \times d

Percentage ionic character

Problem. A diatomic molecule has μ = 1.2 D and bond length 1.0 Å. Find its percentage ionic character (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, 1 D = 3.33 × 10⁻³⁰ C m).

Solution. If fully ionic, μ = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 1.6 × 10⁻²⁹ C m = 4.8 D. % ionic = 1.2/4.8 × 100 = 25 %. (Shortcut: e × 1 Å = 4.8 D.)

Ionic character in covalent bonds and Fajans' rules

Every polar covalent bond has some ionic character; a large electronegativity difference (Δχ about 1.7 or more on the Pauling scale) makes a bond mainly ionic.

Conversely, an ionic bond has some covalent character when the cation polarises (distorts) the electron cloud of the anion. Fajans' rules — covalent character increases when:

Factor Example
the cation is small LiCl is more covalent than NaCl; BeCl₂ is covalent
the cation charge is high NaCl < MgCl₂ < AlCl₃ in covalent character
the anion is large LiI > LiBr > LiCl > LiF
the anion charge is high covalent character rises from F⁻ to O²⁻ to N³⁻
the cation has a pseudo-noble-gas (18-electron) shell CuCl is more covalent than NaCl although Cu⁺ and Na⁺ are similar in size

More covalent character means a lower melting point and better solubility in organic solvents: NaCl (801 °C) > MgCl₂ (714 °C) > AlCl₃ (sublimes near 180 °C).

Bond length, bond order and bond energy

Bond length is the equilibrium distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms. It decreases as bond order increases, as the atoms get smaller and as the s character of the hybrid orbitals increases; bond energy moves the other way.

Bond C–C benzene C–C (order 1.5) C=C C≡C C–H (sp³ / sp² / sp)
Length (pm) 154 139 134 120 109 / 108 / 106

In a molecule with resonance (O₃, NO₃⁻, CO₃²⁻, benzene) all the equivalent bonds have the same intermediate length — the real structure is a hybrid of the Lewis structures, and the bond order is averaged (C–O bond order 4/3 in CO₃²⁻).

Halogen bond energies are an exam favourite: Cl–Cl (243) > Br–Br (193) > F–F (158) > I–I (151 kJ mol⁻¹); F–F is abnormally weak because the lone pairs on the two small F atoms repel each other.

4.4 Hydrogen bonding, metallic bonding and van der Waals forces

Hydrogen bonding

Hydrogen bond

A hydrogen bond is the attraction between a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to a small, highly electronegative atom (F, O or N) and a lone pair on another such atom: X–H···Y.

It is much weaker than a covalent bond (about 10–40 kJ mol⁻¹ against about 400) but stronger than van der Waals forces.

  • Intermolecular hydrogen bonds join different molecules (H₂O, HF, NH₃, alcohols, carboxylic acids — which form dimers): they raise boiling points, viscosity and solubility in water.
  • Intramolecular hydrogen bonds form within one molecule (o-nitrophenol, salicylaldehyde, salicylic acid): they lower the boiling point and the solubility, because the molecule's own H-bond is no longer available to its neighbours — o-nitrophenol is steam-volatile, p-nitrophenol is not.

Effects to quote: H₂O (100 °C), HF (19.5 °C) and NH₃ (−33 °C) boil far above the hydrides of the next elements; ice is less dense than water because each water molecule is hydrogen-bonded tetrahedrally to four others in an open cage, which collapses partly on melting (water is densest at 4 °C); ethanol, glucose and ammonia dissolve in water; HF is a weak acid and forms the HF₂⁻ ion (KHF₂); the double helix of DNA and the α-helix of proteins are held by hydrogen bonds.

Water boils higher than HF although F–H···F is the stronger bond, because each H₂O molecule averages two hydrogen bonds (two H atoms and two lone pairs) while HF averages one.

Metallic bonding

In the electron sea (electron gas) model, a metal is a lattice of positive ions (kernels) immersed in a "sea" of valence electrons that belong to the whole crystal and move freely.

The attraction between the kernels and the mobile electrons is the metallic bond.

It explains electrical and thermal conductivity (mobile electrons), lustre, malleability and ductility (layers of kernels slide without breaking the bond) and generally high melting points.

The bond is stronger with more valence electrons and smaller kernels: m.p. Na 98 °C < Mg 650 °C < Al 660 °C, and Li 181 °C > Na 98 °C > K 63 °C.

Transition metals, with many d electrons available, are very hard and high melting; mercury, with a tightly held 6s² pair, is a liquid.

van der Waals forces

van der Waals forces are the weak attractions between molecules (and noble-gas atoms):

Type Between Example
Dipole–dipole (Keesom) polar molecules HCl, SO₂, CH₃Cl
Dipole–induced dipole (Debye) a polar and a non-polar molecule HCl with Ar; O₂ dissolved in water
London (dispersion) forces all molecules, the only force between non-polar ones; due to momentary dipoles noble gases, H₂, Cl₂, I₂, CH₄
Ion–dipole (not van der Waals, but often asked with them) an ion and a polar molecule Na⁺ hydrated by water

London forces grow with the size of the electron cloud (molar mass, polarisability) and with the surface area of contact.

Hence the boiling points rise He < Ne < Ar < Kr < Xe; F₂ and Cl₂ are gases, Br₂ a liquid and I₂ a solid at room temperature; and among isomers, branching lowers the boiling point: n-pentane (36 °C) > isopentane (28 °C) > neopentane (9.5 °C).

Force Typical energy (kJ mol⁻¹)
Ionic bonding (lattice energy) about 600–4000
Covalent bond about 150–1000
Metallic bonding (enthalpy of atomisation) about 60–850
Hydrogen bond about 10–40
van der Waals forces below about 10
Hydrogen bonds need F, O or N

An ordinary C–H hydrogen (as in CH₄) is not polar enough to form hydrogen bonds — that is why CH₄ fits the normal boiling-point trend while NH₃, H₂O and HF do not.

(Only when carbon carries strongly electron-withdrawing groups, as in CHCl₃, can a weak C–H···O bond form — chloroform with acetone.) And a hydrogen bond lies between an H on one electronegative atom and a lone pair on another; HCl, with a large, less electronegative Cl, forms only dipole–dipole attractions.

Bond angles: CH₄ 109.5°, NH₃ 107°, H₂O 104.5°, NF₃ 102°, PH₃ 93.5°, H₂S 92°, SO₂ 119°, O₃ 117°. Dipole moments: μ = 0 for CO₂, BF₃, CH₄, CCl₄, PCl₅, SF₆, XeF₄; H₂O 1.85 D, NH₃ 1.47 D, NF₃ 0.23 D. Boiling points: H₂O 100 °C > HF 19.5 °C > NH₃ −33 °C.

Chapter summary

  • Atoms bond to reach a noble-gas configuration: ionic (transfer), covalent (sharing), coordinate (a pair donated by one atom — NH₄⁺, H₃O⁺, H₃N→BF₃). The octet rule fails for BF₃, PCl₅, SF₆, NO and xenon fluorides.
  • Formal charge = V − L − B/2; the best Lewis structure minimises formal charges.
  • VSEPR: shape from the steric number SN = ½(V + M − c + a); lp–lp > lp–bp > bp–bp squeezes angles: CH₄ 109.5° > NH₃ 107° > H₂O 104.5°.
  • Lone pairs in a trigonal bipyramid go equatorial: SF₄ see-saw, ClF₃ T-shaped, XeF₂ linear; XeF₄ is square planar.
  • σ bonds come from head-on overlap, π bonds from sideways overlap; double = σ + π, triple = σ + 2π. Hybridisation sp, sp², sp³, sp³d, sp³d², sp³d³ for SN 2–7; more s character, shorter and stronger bond.
  • μ = q × d (debye); symmetric molecules have μ = 0; NH₃ > NF₃; % ionic character = μ(obs)/(e × d) × 100. Fajans: small, highly charged cations and large anions raise covalent character.
  • Bond length falls as bond order and s character rise; resonance makes equivalent bonds equal.
  • Hydrogen bonds (F, O, N) explain the high boiling points of H₂O, HF and NH₃, ice floating and o-nitrophenol's volatility; metallic bonds are an electron sea; London forces grow with size and surface area.

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (d) — The Kossel–Lewis theory: atoms transfer or share electrons to reach an octet (or duplet), the configuration of a noble gas.

2. (b) — In NH₄⁺ the nitrogen lone pair is donated to H⁺. CH₄ and H₂O have ordinary covalent bonds; NaCl is ionic.

3. (a) — SN 4 with no lone pair gives a tetrahedron (CH₄). Square planar needs two lone pairs on an SN of 6.

4. (c) — 109.5° (109° 28′). 104.5° is water, 120° trigonal planar, 90° octahedral.

5. (b) — Each C forms two σ bonds (to C and H) and two π bonds: SN 2, sp, linear.

6. (d) — Lone pairs are held by one nucleus only, spread wider and repel most.

7. (a) — Sideways (lateral) overlap of parallel p orbitals; head-on overlap gives σ bonds.

8. (c) — The debye, 1 D = 3.33 × 10⁻³⁰ C m. The SI unit is the coulomb metre, not the coulomb.

9. (a) — CO₂ is linear, so its two C=O moments cancel. Bent H₂O, pyramidal NH₃ and HCl are polar.

10. (d) — Only F, O and N are small and electronegative enough to leave H strongly δ+ and to offer a compact lone pair.

11. (c) — In ice each molecule is H-bonded tetrahedrally to four others, an open, low-density cage; water is densest at 4 °C, not 0 °C.

12. (b) — Metal kernels in a sea of mobile valence electrons (Drude–Lorentz model).

13. (c) — Momentary dipoles inducing dipoles: London (dispersion) forces, the only attraction between non-polar particles.

14. (a) — SN = ½(6 + 6) = 6, no lone pair: octahedral, all angles 90°.

15. (d) — SN = ½(5 + 5) = 5: sp³d, trigonal bipyramidal.

16. (b) — Boron in BF₃ has only six electrons round it (incomplete octet).

17. (a) — The ions must be free to move: in the melt or in solution. In the solid they are locked in the lattice.

18. (c) — C≡C 120 pm < C=C 134 pm < benzene 139 pm < C–C 154 pm: higher bond order, shorter bond.

19. (d) — N≡N is one σ and two π bonds.

20. (b) — A small, highly charged cation polarises the anion strongly. Noble-gas cations polarise less than pseudo-noble-gas ones of the same size.

13. (b) — Bigger atoms have bigger, more polarisable electron clouds, so the momentary dipoles and London forces are larger.

14. (c) — All have one valence electron; as the kernel grows, the mobile electrons are farther from it and the metallic bond weakens (Li 181 °C, Cs 28 °C).

Model answer D1: VSEPR theory and hybridisation (10 marks)

Introduction. The VSEPR theory (Sidgwick-Powell, Gillespie-Nyholm) says that the shape of a molecule depends on the repulsion between the electron pairs in the valence shell of the central atom.

The repulsion order is lone pair-lone pair > lone pair-bond pair > bond pair-bond pair.

Hybridisation. The mixing of atomic orbitals of nearly equal energy to form the same number of equivalent hybrid orbitals. The type is found from the steric number (bond pairs + lone pairs).

Steric number Hybridisation Lone pairs Shape Bond angle Example
2 sp 0 linear 180^{\circ} BeCl₂, CO₂
3 sp² 0 trigonal planar 120^{\circ} BF₃
3 sp² 1 bent <120^{\circ} SO₂
4 sp³ 0 tetrahedral 109.5^{\circ} CH₄
4 sp³ 1 pyramidal 107^{\circ} NH₃
4 sp³ 2 bent 104.5^{\circ} H₂O
5 sp³d 0 trigonal bipyramidal 90^{\circ}, 120^{\circ} PCl₅
5 sp³d 2 T-shaped / linear ClF₃ / XeF₂
6 sp³d² 0 octahedral 90^{\circ} SF₆
6 sp³d² 2 square planar 90^{\circ} XeF₄

Explaining the angles. In CH₄, NH₃ and H₂O the central atom is sp³ in all three, but lone pairs repel more than bond pairs, so the angle drops from 109.5^{\circ} to 107^{\circ} and 104.5^{\circ}.

Sigma and pi bonds. A sigma (\sigma) bond is formed by head-on overlap and a pi (\pi) bond by sideways overlap of p orbitals. A double bond is 1\sigma + 1\pi and a triple bond is 1\sigma + 2\pi.

Ethene C₂H₄ has 5\sigma + 1\pi and sp² carbons, ethyne C₂H₂ has 3\sigma + 2\pi and sp carbons.

Counting. The steric number = \tfrac12(V + M - C + A), where V is the valence electrons of the central atom, M the monovalent atoms, C the cationic charge and A the anionic charge. For NH₄⁺: \tfrac12(5 + 4 - 1) = 4, sp³, tetrahedral.

For SF₄: \tfrac12(6 + 4) = 5, sp³d, seesaw. For XeF₄: \tfrac12(8 + 4) = 6, sp³d², square planar.

Conclusion. The steric number gives the hybridisation and the arrangement of electron pairs, and the lone pairs squeeze the angles below the ideal values.

Model answer D2: molecular orbital theory and types of bond (10 marks)

Introduction. In MO theory, atomic orbitals combine to form molecular orbitals: a lower-energy bonding MO (\sigma, \pi) and a higher-energy antibonding MO (\sigma^*, \pi^*). The number of MOs equals the number of AOs combined.

Rules. Fill by the Aufbau, Pauli and Hund rules. Bond order = \tfrac12(N_b - N_a). A bond order greater than 0 means the molecule is stable. A higher bond order means a shorter, stronger bond.

Energy order.

  1. For O₂, F₂ and Ne₂: \sigma_{1s} < \sigma^*_{1s} < \sigma_{2s} < \sigma^*_{2s} < \sigma_{2p_z} < \pi_{2p_x} = \pi_{2p_y} < \pi^*_{2p_x} = \pi^*_{2p_y} < \sigma^*_{2p_z}.
  2. For B₂, C₂ and N₂ and lighter, the \pi_{2p} levels lie below \sigma_{2p_z} (s-p mixing).
Species Valence electrons Bond order Magnetism
N₂ 10 3 diamagnetic
O₂ 12 2 paramagnetic (two unpaired electrons in \pi^*)
O₂⁺ 11 2.5 paramagnetic
O₂⁻ (superoxide) 13 1.5 paramagnetic
O₂²⁻ (peroxide) 14 1 diamagnetic
He₂ 4 0 does not exist

The order of bond length is O₂⁺ < O₂ < O₂⁻ < O₂²⁻. The paramagnetism of liquid oxygen, which sticks to a magnet, is explained by MO theory and not by Lewis structures.

Types of bond.

Feature Ionic Covalent Metallic
Formation transfer of electrons sharing of electrons sea of delocalised electrons
Melting point high low (molecular) variable, usually high
Conductivity molten or dissolved poor good
Example NaCl CH₄ Cu

Ionic compounds form easily with a large electronegativity difference, low ionisation enthalpy, high electron gain enthalpy and high lattice enthalpy.

By Fajans' rules, a small cation, a large anion and a high charge increase covalent character (AgCl is more covalent than NaCl).

Numerical. For O₂ the valence MO occupancy is \sigma_{2s}^2\sigma_{2s}^{*2}\sigma_{2p}^2\pi_{2p}^4\pi_{2p}^{*2}, so N_b = 8, N_a = 4 and the bond order is \tfrac12(8 - 4) = 2. For N₂, N_b = 8, N_a = 2 and the bond order is 3.

Conclusion. MO theory predicts bond order and magnetism correctly, and the bond type of any compound depends on electronegativity difference and polarisation.
